questions.prompt: Which statement best describes catabolic pathways per Campbell? ((§9.1, p.165))

options.text: They release stored energy by breaking down complex molecules.
They consume ATP to build macromolecules from smaller subunits.
They always require oxygen as a reactant in every reaction.
They store energy by assembling complex molecules from CO2.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.165). Catabolic pathways release stored energy by breaking down complex molecules.

questions.prompt: How does fermentation differ from aerobic respiration in Concept 9.1? ((§9.1, p.165))

options.text: Fermentation is a partial degradation of sugars or other organic fuel that occurs without oxygen.
Fermentation fully oxidizes glucose to CO2 using an electron transport chain.
Fermentation requires oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor.
Fermentation produces about 32 ATP per glucose under standard conditions.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.165). Fermentation is partial degradation without O2; aerobic respiration is the most efficient pathway and consumes O2.

questions.prompt: In the summary equation for aerobic respiration of glucose, which statement is accurate? ((§9.1, p.165))

options.text: Glucose is oxidized to CO2 and oxygen is reduced to H2O, releasing energy as ATP and heat.
Oxygen is oxidized to CO2 while glucose is reduced to water.
Glucose is reduced to CO2 while oxygen is oxidized to ATP.
Both glucose and oxygen are reduced, producing only heat and no ATP.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.165–166). C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + Energy (ATP + heat); glucose oxidized, O2 reduced.

questions.prompt: What does ΔG = −686 kcal/mol for glucose breakdown indicate? ((§9.1, p.165))

options.text: The reaction is exergonic; products store less energy than reactants and can occur spontaneously.
The reaction is endergonic and requires continuous input of ATP to proceed.
The reaction stores 686 kcal/mol in the products relative to the reactants.
The reaction cannot occur without an electron transport chain.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.165). Negative ΔG means exergonic; products store less energy than reactants.

questions.prompt: In redox terms, oxidation and reduction mean which of the following? ((§9.1, p.166))

options.text: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is addition of electrons to another substance.
Oxidation is gain of electrons; reduction is loss of electrons.
Oxidation is gain of protons only; reduction is loss of neutrons.
Oxidation requires O2 specifically; reduction never involves electron transfer.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.166). Oxidation = loss of e−; reduction = addition of e−.

questions.prompt: In a redox reaction, the reducing agent is best described as which? ((§9.1, p.166))

options.text: The electron donor, which reduces the electron acceptor.
The electron acceptor, which oxidizes the electron donor.
Any molecule that contains oxygen atoms.
The final product that stores the highest free energy.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.166). Reducing agent = electron donor; oxidizing agent = electron acceptor.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of NAD+ during cellular respiration? ((§9.1, p.167))

options.text: It functions as an oxidizing agent that accepts electrons (becoming NADH) from food molecules.
It is the terminal electron acceptor that forms water at the end of the chain.
It directly phosphorylates ADP to ATP in the cytosol.
It pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane by itself.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.167). NAD+ cycles as an oxidizing agent; reduced form is NADH.

questions.prompt: When a dehydrogenase oxidizes a substrate using NAD+, what is delivered to NAD+? ((§9.1, p.167))

options.text: 2 electrons and 1 proton, forming NADH; the other proton is released as H+ into solution.
2 electrons and 2 protons that both remain bound as NADH2.
Only a phosphate group transferred to make NADP+.
Only heat energy with no electron transfer.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.167). Dehydrogenase removes 2 e− and 2 H+; delivers 2 e− + 1 H+ to NAD+.

questions.prompt: Most electrons removed from food travel along which path during aerobic respiration? ((§9.1, p.168))

options.text: glucose → NADH → electron transport chain → oxygen
glucose → O2 → NADH → ATP synthase
glucose → FAD only → cytosol → CO2
glucose → ATP → NAD+ → fermentation products only

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.168). Most electrons travel glucose → NADH → ETC → oxygen.

questions.prompt: According to the chapter preview of ATP accounting, which is accurate? ((§9.1, p.169))

options.text: Oxidative phosphorylation accounts for almost 90% of the ATP generated by respiration.
Substrate-level phosphorylation alone produces almost 90% of cellular ATP.
Glycolysis alone produces about 32 ATP per glucose.
Fermentation produces more ATP per glucose than oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.1, p.169). Oxidative phosphorylation accounts for almost 90% of ATP from respiration; up to about 32 ATP per glucose total.

questions.prompt: What does glycolysis literally refer to, and what are its products from one glucose? ((§9.2, p.170))

options.text: Sugar splitting: glucose is converted to two molecules of pyruvate.
Sugar building: two pyruvates join to form one glucose.
Fat splitting: fatty acids are converted to glycerol only.
Protein splitting: amino acids are deaminated to ammonia.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.170). Glycolysis means sugar splitting; glucose → two pyruvate.

questions.prompt: Where does glycolysis occur in eukaryotic cells? ((§9.2, p.170))

options.text: In the cytosol.
In the mitochondrial matrix.
In the intermembrane space.
In the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.170). Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol.

questions.prompt: What is the net yield of glycolysis per glucose molecule? ((§9.2, p.170))

options.text: 2 ATP and 2 NADH (plus 2 pyruvate and 2 H2O).
4 ATP and 4 NADH with no pyruvate formed.
32 ATP produced entirely by substrate-level phosphorylation.
2 ATP, 6 NADH, and 2 FADH2.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.170). Net: 2 ATP + 2 NADH; also 2 pyruvate + 2 H2O.

questions.prompt: Is carbon dioxide released during glycolysis? ((§9.2, p.170))

options.text: No; all carbon from glucose remains in the two pyruvate molecules.
Yes; three CO2 are released during the investment phase.
Yes; CO2 is released when hexokinase phosphorylates glucose.
Only if oxygen is present in the cytosol.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.170). No CO2 released during glycolysis; carbons remain in the two pyruvates.

questions.prompt: Does glycolysis require oxygen? ((§9.2, p.170))

options.text: No; glycolysis occurs whether or not O2 is present.
Yes; oxygen must accept electrons at the end of glycolysis.
Yes; without O2, hexokinase cannot function.
Only the payoff phase requires oxygen.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.170). Glycolysis occurs with or without O2.

questions.prompt: In the energy investment phase of glycolysis, what happens? ((§9.2, p.170))

options.text: The cell spends 2 ATP; glucose is phosphorylated and split into two 3-carbon sugars.
The cell gains a net of 4 ATP with no ATP spent.
Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion by active transport.
Oxygen is reduced to water in the cytosol.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.170). Investment phase spends 2 ATP.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme catalyzes the second ATP investment of glycolysis and is a key regulatory step? ((§9.2, p.170))

options.text: Phosphofructokinase, transferring a phosphate from ATP to form fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.
Hexokinase, forming glucose 6-phosphate as the only regulated step.
Pyruvate kinase, forming PEP from 2-phosphoglycerate.
Aldolase, joining two trioses into a hexose.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.170). Step 3: phosphofructokinase; second ATP invested; key regulatory step.

questions.prompt: What does hexokinase accomplish in step 1 of glycolysis? ((§9.2, p.170))

options.text: It transfers a phosphate from ATP to glucose, forming glucose 6-phosphate and helping trap the sugar in the cell.
It cleaves fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into G3P and DHAP.
It reduces NAD+ to NADH using electrons from pyruvate.
It converts PEP directly to acetyl CoA.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.170). Hexokinase: glucose → glucose 6-phosphate; charged phosphate traps sugar.

questions.prompt: During the energy payoff phase, how is ATP formed? ((§9.2, p.171))

options.text: By substrate-level phosphorylation (for example, from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and from PEP).
By chemiosmosis at ATP synthase in the cytosol.
By oxidative phosphorylation using Complex IV.
By direct transfer of electrons from NADH to ADP.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.171). Payoff ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation (steps 7 and 10).

questions.prompt: In glycolysis step 6, which molecule is the oxidizing agent? ((§9.2, p.171))

options.text: NAD+, which is reduced to NADH as G3P is oxidized.
G3P, which oxidizes NAD+ to NADH.
Oxygen, which accepts electrons from G3P.
ATP, which oxidizes glucose 6-phosphate.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.2, p.171). Concept Check: oxidizing agent is NAD+; reducing agent is G3P.

questions.prompt: In eukaryotes with O2 present, what happens to pyruvate after glycolysis? ((§9.3, p.171))

options.text: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion by active transport and is converted to acetyl CoA before the citric acid cycle.
Pyruvate remains in the cytosol and is converted directly to citrate.
Pyruvate is immediately fermented to ethanol in all aerobic cells.
Pyruvate is pumped into the nucleus for DNA synthesis.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.171). Pyruvate enters mitochondrion by active transport → acetyl CoA.

questions.prompt: When is the first CO2 of respiration released from pyruvate? ((§9.3, p.171))

options.text: During pyruvate oxidation, when pyruvate’s carboxyl group is removed as CO2.
During glycolysis step 1 when hexokinase acts.
Only after oxidative phosphorylation is complete.
During alcohol fermentation exclusively, never in aerobic respiration.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.171). First CO2 released when carboxyl group removed from pyruvate.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly summarizes pyruvate → acetyl CoA? ((§9.3, p.171))

options.text: Remove carboxyl as CO2; oxidize the remaining 2-carbon fragment (NAD+ → NADH); attach CoA via its sulfur atom.
Attach CoA first, then add two carbons from CO2, then reduce FAD.
Reduce pyruvate with NADH to lactate, then add CoA.
Split pyruvate into three one-carbon CO2 molecules before CoA attaches.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.171 / Fig. 9.9). Three-step pyruvate dehydrogenase conversion.

questions.prompt: The citric acid cycle is also known as which of the following? ((§9.3, p.172))

options.text: The tricarboxylic acid cycle or the Krebs cycle.
The Calvin cycle or the light reactions.
The Cori cycle only.
Beta oxidation of fatty acids.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.172). Also called TCA cycle or Krebs cycle.

questions.prompt: Per turn of the citric acid cycle, how do carbons enter and leave? ((§9.3, p.172))

options.text: Two carbons enter as an acetyl group; two different carbons leave as CO2 in later steps.
Six carbons enter as glucose and leave immediately as six CO2 in one step.
No carbons leave as CO2 until fermentation.
Four carbons enter as oxaloacetate and leave as four CO2 each turn.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.172). 2 C enter as acetyl; 2 C leave as CO2 (steps 3 and 4).

questions.prompt: What is produced per acetyl group (one turn of the citric acid cycle)? ((§9.3, p.172))

options.text: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP (or equivalent) by substrate-level phosphorylation.
2 ATP only, with no electron carriers reduced.
6 NADH and 2 FADH2 with no substrate-level ATP.
32 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation inside the cycle itself.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.172). Per turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP (or GTP equivalent).

questions.prompt: For one glucose, after two turns of the cycle, which carrier totals are correct? ((§9.3, p.172))

options.text: 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, and 2 ATP (or equivalents) from the cycle itself.
3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP total for the whole glucose.
8 FADH2 and no NADH.
Only 2 NADH from the cycle and nothing else.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.172). Per glucose (two turns): 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 ATP.

questions.prompt: What joins the acetyl group of acetyl CoA at the start of the cycle? ((§9.3, p.173))

options.text: Oxaloacetate (4C), forming citrate (6C).
Pyruvate (3C), forming glucose (6C).
Succinate (4C), forming fumarate immediately.
RuBP, forming a 3-carbon sugar.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.173 / Fig. 9.11). Acetyl joins oxaloacetate → citrate.

questions.prompt: Where are most citric acid cycle enzymes located in eukaryotes? ((§9.3, p.173))

options.text: In the mitochondrial matrix (except the step-6 enzyme in the inner membrane).
Entirely in the cytosol like glycolysis.
Only in the intermembrane space.
In the nucleus next to ATP synthase.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.3, p.173 / Fig. 9.11 caption). Most enzymes in matrix; step 6 enzyme in inner membrane.

questions.prompt: Glycolysis plus the citric acid cycle together yield how many ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose? ((§9.3, p.174))

options.text: 4 ATP (2 net from glycolysis + 2 from the cycle).
About 32 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation alone.
Zero ATP until oxidative phosphorylation begins.
16 ATP from glycolysis alone.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.174). Glycolysis + citric acid cycle yield only 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.prompt: Where is the electron transport chain embedded in eukaryotic cells? ((§9.4, p.174))

options.text: In the inner mitochondrial membrane.
In the outer mitochondrial membrane only.
Freely dissolved in the cytosol.
In the nuclear envelope.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.174). ETC in inner mitochondrial membrane (plasma membrane in prokaryotes).

questions.prompt: How do NADH and FADH2 differ in feeding electrons to the ETC? ((§9.4, p.174))

options.text: NADH donates electrons at Complex I; FADH2 donates at Complex II at a lower energy level.
Both donate electrons only at Complex IV.
FADH2 donates at Complex I while NADH donates at Complex II.
Neither interacts with membrane complexes; both reduce O2 directly in the matrix.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.174–175). NADH → Complex I; FADH2 → Complex II.

questions.prompt: Which statement about ubiquinone (Q / CoQ) is accurate? ((§9.4, p.174))

options.text: It is a small hydrophobic molecule and the only electron transport chain member that is not a protein.
It is a cytochrome with a heme group that reduces O2 directly.
It is restricted to the cytosol and never enters membranes.
It is identical to ATP synthase’s catalytic knob.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.174–175). Q is the only nonprotein ETC member.

questions.prompt: Does the electron transport chain make ATP directly? ((§9.4, p.175))

options.text: No; it breaks the free-energy drop into smaller steps and establishes a proton gradient used later for ATP synthesis.
Yes; each complex phosphorylates ADP as electrons pass.
Yes; Complex II alone synthesizes all cellular ATP.
Only when fermentation is also running.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.175). ETC makes no ATP directly.

questions.prompt: What is chemiosmosis in this chapter’s sense? ((§9.4, p.175))

options.text: Energy stored in an H+ gradient across a membrane drives cellular work such as ATP synthesis.
Direct transfer of a phosphate from a substrate molecule to ADP only.
Diffusion of glucose across the outer membrane without transporters.
Binding of O2 to hemoglobin in the blood.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.175–176). Chemiosmosis: H+ gradient drives work (ATP synthesis).

questions.prompt: During electron transport, H+ are pumped in which direction in mitochondria? ((§9.4, p.176))

options.text: From the matrix into the intermembrane space, creating a proton-motive force.
From the intermembrane space into the matrix only, eliminating any gradient.
From the cytosol into the nucleus.
Equally in both directions so no gradient forms.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.176). ETC pumps H+ matrix → intermembrane space.

questions.prompt: How do protons return to the matrix to drive ATP synthesis? ((§9.4, p.176))

options.text: Through ATP synthase, the only route for H+ to diffuse back down their gradient across the inner membrane.
Through Complex II exclusively, bypassing ATP synthase.
Through open porins that leak all gradients instantly.
Through hexokinase in the cytosol.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.176). ATP synthase is the route for H+ reentry coupled to ATP synthesis.

questions.prompt: Oxidative phosphorylation consists of which processes? ((§9.4, p.176))

options.text: Electron transport plus chemiosmosis.
Glycolysis plus alcohol fermentation only.
Pyruvate oxidation without any membrane involvement.
The Calvin cycle plus photorespiration.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.176). Oxidative phosphorylation = electron transport + chemiosmosis.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate maximum ATP yield per glucose from cellular respiration in this chapter? ((§9.4, p.177))

options.text: About 30 or 32 ATP, depending largely on the shuttle that transfers electrons from cytosolic NADH.
Exactly 2 ATP from fermentation pathways only.
Exactly 4 ATP with no contribution from oxidative phosphorylation.
About 686 ATP, one per kcal/mol of glucose.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.177). Maximum ≈ 30 or 32 ATP per glucose.

questions.prompt: About what fraction of the energy in glucose is transferred to ATP under the book’s accounting? ((§9.4, p.178))

options.text: About 34% (most of the rest is lost as heat).
About 100%, with no heat loss.
About 2%, because only glycolysis counts.
About 90% stored permanently in NADH without ATP formation.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.4, p.178). Efficiency ≈ 34% transferred to ATP; remainder as heat.

questions.prompt: What is a key contrast between anaerobic respiration and fermentation? ((§9.5, p.179))

options.text: Anaerobic respiration uses an electron transport chain; fermentation does not.
Fermentation uses an ETC ending at O2; anaerobic respiration never transfers electrons.
Both require O2 as the terminal electron acceptor.
Fermentation produces ~32 ATP while anaerobic respiration produces 2 ATP.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.179). Anaerobic respiration uses an ETC; fermentation does not.

questions.prompt: In the book’s example of anaerobic respiration, sulfate-reducing marine bacteria use which final electron acceptor? ((§9.5, p.179))

options.text: SO4^2−, producing H2S as a by-product (instead of H2O).
O2, producing only water.
Nitrogen gas exclusively, producing ammonia in all cases.
Pyruvate, producing lactate in the mitochondrion.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.179). Final acceptor SO4^2−; by-product H2S.

questions.prompt: Why must NAD+ be regenerated during fermentation? ((§9.5, p.180))

options.text: Without regenerating NAD+ from NADH, glycolysis would stop for lack of an oxidizing agent.
NAD+ is needed only for ATP synthase rotation.
NAD+ must be converted permanently to CO2.
Fermentation consumes NAD+ as a fuel molecule instead of glucose.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.180). Glycolysis needs NAD+ as oxidizing agent; fermentation regenerates it.

questions.prompt: In alcohol fermentation, what are the two steps after glycolysis? ((§9.5, p.180))

options.text: Pyruvate releases CO2 to form acetaldehyde; acetaldehyde is reduced by NADH to ethanol, regenerating NAD+.
Pyruvate is reduced directly to lactate with no CO2 released.
Acetaldehyde is oxidized to pyruvate using O2.
Ethanol is phosphorylated to form glucose 6-phosphate.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.180 / Fig. 9.16a). CO2 → acetaldehyde; NADH reduces acetaldehyde → ethanol.

questions.prompt: How does lactic acid fermentation differ from alcohol fermentation? ((§9.5, p.180))

options.text: Pyruvate is reduced directly by NADH to lactate, and no CO2 is released.
Lactate fermentation always releases two CO2 before reducing acetaldehyde.
Lactate fermentation requires an electron transport chain ending at sulfate.
Lactate fermentation occurs only in yeast used for bread.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.180 / Fig. 9.16b). Direct reduction to lactate; no CO2.

questions.prompt: In fermentation versus cellular respiration, how does NADH get oxidized back to NAD+? ((§9.5, p.181))

options.text: Fermentation: an organic molecule (e.g., pyruvate or acetaldehyde) is the final acceptor; respiration: electrons go to an electron transport chain.
Both always use O2 as the only possible final acceptor.
Fermentation sends electrons to Complex IV; respiration reduces pyruvate.
Neither pathway regenerates NAD+ under any conditions.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.181). Key difference is how NADH is oxidized back to NAD+.

questions.prompt: Relative to fermentation, about how much ATP can aerobic respiration yield per glucose? ((§9.5, p.181))

options.text: Up to about 32 ATP — roughly 16× as much as fermentation’s net 2 ATP.
Exactly the same 2 ATP net with no additional yield.
About half as much ATP as fermentation.
Unlimited ATP because O2 creates energy from nothing.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.181). Aerobic respiration up to ~32 ATP ≈ 16× fermentation.

questions.prompt: What characterizes obligate anaerobes? ((§9.5, p.181))

options.text: They carry out only fermentation or anaerobic respiration and cannot survive in O2 (which can be toxic).
They require O2 and die without an electron transport chain ending at oxygen.
They perform only photosynthesis in bright light.
They live exclusively in vertebrate brain tissue.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.181). Obligate anaerobes: fermentation/anaerobic respiration only; O2 can be toxic.

questions.prompt: What can facultative anaerobes such as yeasts do? ((§9.5, p.181))

options.text: Make enough ATP by fermentation or by respiration, with pyruvate as a fork in the metabolic road.
Survive only when O2 is completely absent forever.
Never use glycolysis under any condition.
Use sulfate as their only possible electron acceptor.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.181 / Fig. 9.17). Facultative anaerobes: fermentation or respiration.

questions.prompt: Why is glycolysis considered evolutionarily ancient in this chapter? ((§9.5, p.182))

options.text: It is widespread, occurs in the cytosol without membrane organelles, and likely existed before appreciable atmospheric O2.
It requires mitochondria and therefore evolved only after eukaryotes appeared.
It depends on oxygen and cyanobacteria exclusively.
It is found only in vertebrate muscle and nowhere else.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.5, p.182). Glycolysis as metabolic heirloom; ancient prokaryotes before O2.

questions.prompt: What roles do glycolysis and the citric acid cycle play for diverse fuels? ((§9.6, p.182))

options.text: They act as major intersections (catabolic funnels) that oxidize intermediates from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
They only process glucose and reject all other organic molecules.
They are used solely for anabolic synthesis and never for ATP.
They occur only in chloroplasts during the day.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.182 / Fig. 9.18). Catabolic funnels for carbs, fats, proteins.

questions.prompt: Before amino acids can be oxidized in glycolysis or the citric acid cycle, what must happen? ((§9.6, p.182))

options.text: They must be deaminated (amino groups removed); nitrogenous waste may be excreted as ammonia, urea, or other products.
They must be converted entirely to starch in the digestive tract.
They must bind irreversibly to ATP synthase.
They must be beta-oxidized into two-carbon fragments first.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.182). Proteins → amino acids → deamination before entry.

questions.prompt: What does beta oxidation do to fatty acids? ((§9.6, p.183))

options.text: Breaks them into two-carbon fragments that enter the citric acid cycle as acetyl CoA (also generating NADH and FADH2).
Converts them directly to pyruvate in glycolysis without acetyl CoA.
Joins them to form glycogen in muscle.
Removes amino groups to form urea.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.183). Beta oxidation → 2-C fragments → acetyl CoA.

questions.prompt: How does fat compare with carbohydrate for ATP yield by mass? ((§9.6, p.183))

options.text: A gram of fat oxidized by respiration yields more than twice as much ATP as a gram of carbohydrate.
A gram of carbohydrate always yields more than twice the ATP of a gram of fat.
Fat and carbohydrate yield identical ATP per gram.
Fat cannot be oxidized by cellular respiration at all.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.183). Fat >2× ATP per gram vs carbohydrate.

questions.prompt: After fat digestion, glycerol enters respiration by conversion to which intermediate? ((§9.6, p.183))

options.text: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (a glycolysis intermediate).
Oxaloacetate in the Calvin cycle.
Lactate in the nucleus.
Citrate synthase in the intermembrane space.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.183). Glycerol → glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.

questions.prompt: Besides fuel, how can food molecules and pathway intermediates be used? ((§9.6, p.183))

options.text: As carbon skeletons for biosynthesis; anabolic pathways consume ATP.
Only as heat with no biosynthetic role.
Exclusively to build O2 from water.
Only after all ATP stores are permanently destroyed.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.183). Intermediates diverted as anabolic precursors; anabolism consumes ATP.

questions.prompt: Regarding amino acid biosynthesis in humans, which statement matches the text? ((§9.6, p.183))

options.text: Humans can make about half of the 20 amino acids from citric acid cycle compounds; essential amino acids must come from the diet.
Humans synthesize all 20 amino acids and never need dietary amino acids.
Humans cannot make any amino acids and must obtain all 20 from fat only.
Essential amino acids are produced only by beta oxidation of glycerol.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.183). About half of 20 amino acids made; essentials from diet.

questions.prompt: What is the most common metabolic control mechanism described for respiration? ((§9.6, p.183))

options.text: Feedback inhibition, in which an end product inhibits an early enzyme in the pathway.
Random destruction of all mitochondria when ATP is low.
Permanent inactivation of NAD+ after one use.
Stimulation of every enzyme equally by high citrate only.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.183). Most common control: feedback inhibition.

questions.prompt: How is phosphofructokinase regulated as the pacemaker of respiration? ((§9.6, p.183))

options.text: It is allosterically stimulated by AMP and inhibited by ATP and citrate.
It is stimulated by ATP and citrate and inhibited by AMP.
It is irreversibly destroyed whenever glucose is present.
It functions only in the mitochondrial matrix, not in glycolysis.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.183–184 / Fig. 9.19). PFK: stimulated by AMP; inhibited by ATP and citrate.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter emphasize about the energy that keeps organisms alive? ((§9.6, p.184))

options.text: Cellular respiration releases energy that was originally stored by photosynthesis; it does not create energy from nothing.
Cellular respiration manufactures new energy that never existed in ecosystems.
All usable energy originates from fermentation of sulfate.
ATP appears spontaneously without prior energy input from food or light.

questions.explanation: Source: Campbell Biology AP 12e, (§9.6, p.184). Energy is released, not produced; originally stored by photosynthesis.
